title: Why acquisitions aren't always failures: independent companies change and fail too
summary: Jason Cohen refutes the claim that every acquisition is a failure. Companies change constantly whether independent or acquired, most startups fail either way, and a well-chosen sale can create liquidity, jobs, and opportunity for founders, employees, and products. He argues the useful question is when acquisition is wise.

principles.text: Companies change constantly; expecting a startup to keep its early 'youthful energy' by staying independent is naive.
principles.quote: A company won't be a band of six people doing whatever they want forever, whether you sell or stay independent.

principles.text: Don't judge an acquisition by the founder's feelings; post-exit sadness is typical even after great exits.
principles.quote: More likely, the typical postpartum depression that naturally follows even the most successful of exits.

principles.text: Judge a deal by what it does for employees too: most people prefer stability, better pay, and new opportunities over founder-style risk.
principles.quote: Most people don't have a founder's temperament for independence and risk. What if those people *wanted* those jobs?

principles.text: Bad outcomes happen at independent companies too; compare acquisition failure rates against the failure rate of staying independent.
principles.quote: People love quoting statistics about how most acquisitions are failures, but they forget to mention that most independent startups also fail

principles.text: A sale can be the right call even if founders later leave; leaving doesn't prove the choice was wrong for them, employees, or the product.
principles.quote: In many of those cases the founders left ahead of others, and yes they went back to founder-y types of activity. That doesn't prove it wasn't the right choice at the time

principles.text: Replace superlatives with the real question: under what conditions is acquisition good for all parties?
principles.quote: we ask "When is acquisition wise?" and "What are the conditions under which acquisitions are likely to be good for all parties?"
